overview.title: Where the ferries and fishing boats meet
overview.p1: Beni Ansar is Nador’s port town: ferry connections, commercial traffic and a working harbour atmosphere that feels different from the corniche cafés.
overview.p2: Visit for the energy of landings and seafood, or as a practical stop if you arrive or leave by sea. It is not a polished tourist marina.
overview.p3: Keep valuables close in busy zones and confirm ferry paperwork well before sailing days.

food.title: Food at Beni Ansar Port
food.p1: One of the best spots near Nador for fresh fish — harbour grills and simple seafood tables when the boats are in.
food.li1: Ask for the day’s catch near the port.
food.li2: Grilled sardines and small fish are local staples.
food.li3: Busy lunch tables often mean fresher turnover.
food.li4: Combine a harbour meal with a short port walk.
food.li5: Confirm prices if menus are not clearly posted.
food.p2: Stronger for seafood than long café evenings — save the corniche for that.

q1.question: Is it only for ferry passengers?
q1.answer: No — the harbour area is interesting for atmosphere even if you are not sailing.

q2.question: Seafood?
q2.answer: Fresh fish is the local draw near the port.

q3.question: How far from the centre?
q3.answer: A short drive east of central Nador.

q4.question: Melilla border?
q4.answer: The Spanish border zone is in the wider area — bring passport if you intend to cross.

q5.question: How long to spend?
q5.answer: One to two hours is enough for a look and a meal stop.
